Issued at 529 AM CDT Thu Jul 30 2026

A series of shortwave troughs is located at the top of a 
central CONUS ridge early this morning. Occasional showers and 
thunderstorms have been observed in North Dakota overnight, 
mainly in Hettinger and Grant Counties and along the Canadian 
border. A deeper shortwave ejecting off the Northern Rockies 
early this morning is forecast to to reach the Northern Plains 
this afternoon. The broad synoptic scale lift is expected to 
result in periods of showers and thunderstorms throughout the 
day, mainly across the southern two thirds of the state and with
probabilities peaking in the afternoon. But CAMs continue to be
highly inconsistent with timing and coverage of convection. 
More recent model initializations (after 00Z) have trended 
toward a much drier outcome until later this afternoon, but this
doesn't seem to fit the conceptual model of modest differential
cyclonic vorticity advection through a deeply moist air mass. 
It does appear there could be forcing assistance from weak upper
level jet dynamics later this afternoon, which may be what 06Z 
and later guidance is honing in on. Whether convection later 
today remains elevated or becomes rooted in the near-surface or 
mixed layer could be strongly dependent on how cloud cover 
influences diurnal heating. But even if there is more sunshine 
than expected, updrafts may still need to overcome a capping 
layer aloft. CAPE is forecast to increase into the 1000-2000 
J/kg range this afternoon, but could be higher if the RAP/NBM 
advertised dewpoints of upper 60s to mid 70s come to fruition. 
Shear at all layers is forecast to remain weak though, with 
effective bulk shear under 30 kts. The weaker shear with a lack 
of a well-defined surface boundary gives high confidence in a 
cluster storm mode with pulse intensity. A few stronger to 
marginally severe storms can still not be ruled out, but the 
threat ceiling should remain closer to baseline severe hazards 
of quarter size hail and wind gusts near 60 mph. It does appear 
there may be a conditional threat for non-supercell tornadoes, 
especially if the boundary layer is able to become unstable. The
conditional aspect of this threat is that it would likely 
require outflow boundary collisions to generate the requisite 
surface vorticity needed for landspouts. This potential will not
be messaged in any of our other products, but is something to 
keep in mind heading into the afternoon. Finally, there is still
a risk for locally excessive rainfall from storms today, with 
anomalously high precipitable water, high deep-layer RH, and the
potential for both training convection and slow storm motions. 
HREF guidance would indicate that a maximum rain amount of 2 to 
4 inches is a reasonable high-end outcome, but the spatial 
coverage of even just +1" is likely to be very limited. 

The shortwave responsible for today's convection is forecast to
dig into the Upper Mississippi River Valley on Friday. A 
trailing, much lower-amplitude shortwave could bring a few 
showers or thunderstorms to western parts of the state 
throughout the day Friday, shifting into northern North Dakota 
Friday night when a low level jet could increase coverage. 
Higher CIN and lower CAPE should prevent severe storms on 
Friday, but if a storm can become rooted in the near- surface 
layer it would have access to as much as 40 kts of effective 
bulk shear. Forecast uncertainty paired with CAM reflectivity 
output precludes messaging of stronger convection at this time.

Today will be much cooler than yesterday, and likely the 
coolest day of the week for most with forecast highs generally 
in the 80s. There continues to be high confidence in the 
upstream upper level ridge re-amplifying and tilting back over 
the Northern Plains through the weekend. Most locations south of
Highway 2 and west of Highway 83 are likely to see at least one
day this weekend with a high temperature of at least 100 
degrees. The triple-digit heat should remain confined to western
parts of the state on Saturday, with spatial extent less 
certain on Sunday because of the timing of a cold front. Areas 
where the front passes through prior to peak heating (most 
likely far northwest North Dakota) could see highs closer to 90 
on Sunday. But areas along and ahead of the cold Sunday 
afternoon (most likely southwest/central North Dakota) could 
easily reach or even exceed 105 degrees with the assistance of 
compressional heating. Not only could heat be an impact this 
weekend, but stronger winds on Sunday could combine with the hot
temperatures and RH as low as 10-15 percent to produce at least
near- critical fire weather conditions.

There is a low chance that showers and thunderstorms could 
develop along the cold front as it moves into central and 
eastern North Dakota later in the day Sunday into Sunday night,
